Summary

AstraSync must decide whether to accept one of the client’s two lower-priced offers (A: $152K per month; B: $125K per month plus an $800K success bonus) or reject both and bid $150K per month in an RFP with a gain-share reward (C). We valued each option as the present value of AstraSync’s contribution over 18 months at 1.5% per month, built a decision tree, and simulated the client’s savings 1,000,000 times to value the gain-share. The options are nearly tied on expected value: C at $509,329, B at $506,713 and A at $501,522. C’s small lead disappears if the chance of winning the RFP falls below 39.8% (the estimate is 40%), and C has a 60% chance of earning nothing. We recommend AstraSync accept Option B, giving up less than 1% of expected value to keep the client and avoid the all-or-nothing RFP.

The three alternatives

AstraSync’s cost is 1,200 hours × $100 = $120,000 per month. Every value below is the present value of revenue minus cost over 18 months at 1.5% per month.

Option A: $152,000 per month. AstraSync earns a certain $32,000 per month, worth $501,522 today. There is no risk.

Option B: $125,000 per month plus an $800,000 bonus at month 18. The monthly margin is only $5,000 ($78,363), but the bonus is paid if the project beats the client’s benchmark, which AstraSync puts at 70%. AstraSync earns $690,292 with the bonus or $78,363 without it, for an expected $506,713.

Option C: reject both and bid $150,000 per month in the RFP. If AstraSync wins (40%), it earns $30,000 per month plus a gain-share at month 18 based on the client’s savings, Triangular($3.2M, $5.6M, $12.8M). The simulated average gain-share is $1,049,984, so winning is worth $1,273,322. Losing (60%) pays $0, for an expected $509,329.

Expected value is not the whole story
Option Expected value Worst outcome Best outcome Chance of $0
A $501,522 $501,522 $501,522 0%
B $506,713 $78,363 $690,292 0%
C $509,329 $0 $3,589,839 60%

The three expected values are within about $7,807 of each other, but the risks are very different: A is certain, B never pays less than $78,363, and C pays nothing 6 times out of 10.

Input 1: probability of winning the RFP
Input 2: probability of earning the Option B bonus
Why these two inputs, and where the answer flips

Both probabilities are estimates rather than facts, and each one decides the ranking between options.

  • P(win RFP): C beats B only above 39.8%. The 40% estimate sits almost on that line, so a slightly more pessimistic view of the competition makes B the better choice.
  • P(bonus): B beats A above 69.2% and beats C above 70.4%. The 70% estimate sits between the two, less than one point from either edge.
Conclusion
AstraSync should accept Option B.

By expected value alone, the RFP (C) ranks first at $509,329, ahead of B at $506,713 and A at $501,522. The gap between C and B is only $2,616, which is small compared with the uncertainty in the inputs.

The sensitivity analysis shows C’s lead depends on a 40% win probability that only needs to slip to 39.8% to disappear. C also carries a 60% chance of earning nothing and losing the client.

Option B keeps the client, guarantees at least $78,363, and pays $690,292 in the 70% case where AstraSync delivers as it expects. It also ties AstraSync’s pay to the client’s results, which helps grow the relationship.

What would change our mind: clear evidence that AstraSync’s chance of winning the RFP is well above 40%, or a bonus probability below 69.2%, at which point Option A’s certain $152K per month becomes the better choice.
